questions.explanation: The `finally` block runs on cancellation, so "cleanup start" prints. But the coroutine is already cancelled, so the `delay(10)` inside `finally` throws CancellationException at once and "cleanup end" is skipped. Suspending cleanup must be wrapped in `withContext(NonCancellable) { }`.

questions.question: What does structured concurrency guarantee?
options: Child coroutines always run on the same thread as their parent, in the order they were launched
A parent doesn't complete until its children do, and cancelling a parent cancels its children
A child that fails is restarted automatically, so the parent never sees the failure
Each coroutine runs in its own isolated scope, so cancelling one never affects any other
questions.explanation: Every coroutine has a parent Job in a tree. A parent waits for its children, cancellation flows down to children, and a failure in a regular child flows up and cancels the parent. Threads and order are decided by dispatchers, and nothing is restarted automatically.

questions.question: Why is `GlobalScope.launch { }` discouraged in Android code?
options: It always runs its coroutines on the main thread, so any long-running work started there freezes the UI
It cancels every other coroutine in the app when one of its coroutines fails
Its coroutines aren't tied to any lifecycle, so they can keep running after the screen is gone
Its coroutines cannot call suspend functions; only those from `CoroutineScope.launch` can
questions.explanation: GlobalScope has no Job, so its coroutines have no parent and are never cancelled by a screen or ViewModel going away. That leaks work and anything it captures, such as views. It uses Dispatchers.Default, not the main thread. Use `viewModelScope`, `lifecycleScope` or an injected scope instead.

questions.question: Wrapping a suspend call in `try { } catch (e: Exception) { }` inside a coroutine can break cancellation, because it also catches CancellationException.
questions.explanation: CancellationException is a subclass of Exception, so a broad catch swallows it and the code continues as if nothing happened. In a loop, that can keep the coroutine busy even after its scope is cancelled. Rethrow CancellationException, or catch only the exception types you expect.

questions.question: A coroutine runs a long CPU loop with no suspend calls. Which changes let it respond to cancellation? Select all that apply.
options: Wrap the loop in `try { } catch (e: Exception) { }`
questions.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative: code only stops at points that check for it. `ensureActive()` throws if cancelled, `yield()` is a suspension point that checks, and `isActive` lets you exit the loop yourself. `Thread.sleep` does not check coroutine cancellation, and a broad catch would swallow the CancellationException.

questions.question: A `launch { withTimeout(1000) { fetch() } }` times out. There is no try/catch and no crash. Why?
options: `withTimeout` returns null on timeout, so the launch body ends normally with no exception
TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, so it counts as cancellation, not failure
The timeout cancels the parent scope first, so by the time it throws the exception has nowhere to go
`launch` catches every exception thrown inside its block and only logs it at debug level in logcat
questions.explanation: TimeoutCancellationException extends CancellationException, and cancellation is never sent to exception handlers or treated as a failure of the parent. So the coroutine just stops. `withTimeoutOrNull` is the version that returns null; with plain `withTimeout` you should catch the exception if you need to react to the timeout.

questions.question: Inside a ViewModel, someone writes `viewModelScope.launch(Job()) { refresh() }`. What is the effect?
options: The `Job()` becomes the parent, so the coroutine leaves viewModelScope and isn't cancelled in `onCleared()`
It makes the coroutine start lazily, so `refresh()` only runs when the Job is started
It has no effect, because a scope always uses its own Job as the parent and ignores the one passed in
It makes the coroutine a supervisor child, so a failure in `refresh()` no longer cancels sibling coroutines
questions.explanation: The context passed to `launch` is added on top of the scope's context, so the explicit `Job()` replaces viewModelScope's Job as the parent. The coroutine is detached from the scope, and clearing the ViewModel will not cancel it. Passing a `Job()` or `SupervisorJob()` directly to a builder is almost always a mistake.
